source.title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether prior acquisition changes later recovery using matched-history relearning during continual fine-tuning, rather than testing an unlearning method or the attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports relearning results for previously learned, matched never-learned, and competing-answer histories. It does not test unlearning methods, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery.
record.test_reason: The forgetting here is not unlearning. It comes from interference in a rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, and it stays partial (ΔL ≈0.38–0.43 nats at k=100; a near-chance recipe was excluded). Relearning trains on the exact target statements, and the measure is savings relative to a matched never-learned binding. Restoration of knowledge an unlearning method had hidden is never measured. Version B names recovery from unlearned models, so the rows measure a related construct: savings after catastrophic forgetting. The authors say they do not claim a new recovery demonstration and cite unlearning work only as related work and broader impact. The reader's T2/tests guess is not adopted; the finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, which the authors say neither establishes equivalence nor rules out a slot contribution. The ~18% figure is a secondary, descriptive, unpaired comparison. The authors frame the contribution as measurement for continual learning, not a new demonstration of recovery after unlearning.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses matched learning histories, a rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, and later answer-token-only fine-tuning on the same target binding; it does not apply a machine-unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported forgetting depth depends on checkpoint sampling density and training recipe; the planned behavioral-equivalence gate was unusable because the JS margin was below measured same-history cross-seed variation. Savings are front-loaded across relearning steps and approach zero by u ≥ 16.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-1.5B, bindings learned and then partially forgotten through a rehearsal-free continual stream relearn faster than exposure-matched never-learned bindings. Two-history mean S is 0.177 nats with all three CIs excluding zero. The rebuild mean is 0.170 (2/3 CIs positive), and the slot-matched WRONG−CONTROL control is null (−0.002). Savings stay positive after baseline adjustment (Table 4). The secondary conversion is ≈0.69 steps, about 18% of naive acquisition cost. Savings hold at 0.18–0.21 from k=50 to k=250.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behaviorally forgotten facts after continual fine-tuning (not unlearning) retain binding-specific relearning savings relative to matched never-learned facts.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents
record.problems: One model at one scale, synthetic facts, and three optimization seeds. Forgetting remains partial and behavioral equivalence between histories is not established. The update-cost comparison uses a separate, unpaired FRESH pool; the three-history conversion borrows its denominator. WRONG combines slot familiarity with competitor interference. The study does not locate a storage mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported findings bearing on version B were left out. Behavioral-forgetting checkpoints and JS calibration results were not entered as recovery rows because they do not measure restoration by fine-tuning.

untested.parts: No unlearning method, near-chance targeted accuracy, general-ability retention, or attack resistance.
No unlearned model. Relearning on unrelated, loosely related, or subset-of-forgotten facts is not tested; relearning uses the target statements themselves.
No activation ablation or storage/access analysis; the authors disclaim locating a mechanism.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to B and labelled supports/limits_scope. Those labels are dropped because the setting is continual-learning forgetting, not unlearning, and the relearning data are the target facts themselves. Behavioral forgetting is only partial (ΔL ≈0.4 nats at k=100), and no unlearning method or general-ability check appears. If curators widen B to cover any behavioral forgetting, the rows would support B in this single-model synthetic setting, with the scope limits the reader listed. This is a workshop paper from a single author.

versions.untested_parts: No unlearning method is evaluated for near-chance targeted accuracy, retained general ability, or resistance to simple attacks.

Tests fine-tuning on two statements that restate the same target binding after partial forgetting. Does not test unrelated or loosely related examples, unlearning methods, or recovery after near-chance behavior.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis locating storage or access in parameters or activations.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context-only recovery.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B, synthetic bindings, partial forgetting at k=100; two-history LEARNED versus matched CONTROL
reader_labels.reason: Previously learned bindings show positive relearning savings in all three seeds; all Table 2 intervals exclude zero (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Three-history rebuild and conversion to update savings
reader_labels.reason: The rebuild LEARNED − CONTROL estimate is weaker in seed 2, and one seed's naive-cost fraction interval includes zero; the evidence is for partial forgetting and same-binding relearning, not near-chance forgetting or unrelated examples (r5–r7, r14–r17).
